findings.claim: `#children` now depends on `createNullObject()` preserving the exact semantics of `Object.create(null)`; if the helper returns a shared/cached object or a normal `{}` literal, this silently breaks per-instance isolation or prototype-pollution safety.
findings.rationale: This field initializer runs once per `Node` instance and the router mutates `#children` by arbitrary path-segment keys. Two failure modes are plausible and not visible in this hunk: (a) if `createNullObject` returns a module-level singleton (a common shape for such a helper, e.g. `const NULL_OBJ = Object.create(null); export const createNullObject = () => NULL_OBJ`), every Node would share one children map and routing would be completely wrong; (b) if it returns `{}` or `Object.assign({}, ...)` rather than a null-prototype object, then route segments named `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, etc. would hit inherited properties — the `node.#children[token]` lookups would return `Object.prototype` members instead of `undefined`, and `__proto__` assignment would be swallowed. The original `Object.create(null)` was almost certainly deliberate for exactly this reason. Medium confidence that there is a real bug (depends on the unseen helper), high confidence this is worth verifying.

findings.claim: The declared type `Record<string, Node>` may no longer be checked if `createNullObject()` returns `any`.
findings.rationale: `Object.create(null)` returns `any` in TypeScript, so the annotation was the only thing giving this field a type; a wrapper that also returns `any` (rather than a generic `createNullObject<T>(): T` or `Record<string, never>`) keeps the same weak-typing hole, and a wrapper returning something narrower (e.g. `Record<string, unknown>`) would fail to assign here. Low-to-medium confidence; worth confirming the helper is generic so the annotation still carries weight.
